Measured relations and operator algebras

Principal groupoids with hidden group factors

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. New original text is public domain (CC0).

A principal groupoid has no nonidentity isotropy arrows. Its measurable structure can nevertheless carry a group coordinate invisible to the unit sigma-field. The preceding binary example gives an abelian random-operator algebra. Here we construct the full countable-group version, classify all its proper transverse functions, and compute a properly infinite factor when the group is the free group on two generators.

The factor example also tests the usual tensor construction of two commuting copies. An explicit controlled translation lies in the relative commutant of one copy and outside the other; the two copies do not generate the tensor-field algebra. This is a failure of that particular construction at the weaker measurable scope. It does not prove that no other endomorphism and symmetry satisfy Connes's Corollary 11. That source assertion remains open at this scope.

We use the fully proved subgroup in Countable generation and isotropy topologies, Theorem 1.2, and its perfect-set lemma. Principal groupoids with extra fibre information supplies the binary predecessor and the random-operator conventions. Ordinary sigma-finite integration, separable Hilbert spaces, the double commutant theorem and Hilbert tensor products are prerequisites. Every measure, kernel, covariance, commutant and factor calculation needed for the present construction is proved below. No group-factor classification, tensor primeness theorem or general modular bridge is imported.

Trivial set-theoretic isotropy, one orbit, sigma-finite transverse measure and a properly infinite factor therefore do not restore standard Borel fibre density. The missing group coordinate is a measurable phenomenon.

Proof. Let TTT commute with all left translations and UUU with all right translations. If c=Tδec=T\delta_ec=Tδe​ and d=Uδed=U\delta_ed=Uδe​, their matrix entries, with output index first, are Tx,z=cz−1xT_{x,z}=c_{z^{-1}x}Tx,z​=cz−1x​ and Ux,z=dxz−1U_{x,z}=d_{xz^{-1}}Ux,z​=dxz−1​. For arbitrary x,zx,zx,z, (TU)x,z=∑ycy−1xdyz−1=∑kckdxk−1z−1,(UT)x,z=∑ydxy−1cz−1y=∑kdxk−1z−1ck.(5A.4) \begin{aligned} (TU)_{x,z} &=\sum_y c_{y^{-1}x}d_{yz^{-1}} =\sum_k c_kd_{xk^{-1}z^{-1}},\\ (UT)_{x,z} &=\sum_y d_{xy^{-1}}c_{z^{-1}y} =\sum_k d_{xk^{-1}z^{-1}}c_k . \end{aligned} \tag{5A.4} (TU)x,z​(UT)x,z​​=y∑​cy−1x​dyz−1​=k∑​ck​dxk−1z−1​,=y∑​dxy−1​cz−1y​=k∑​dxk−1z−1​ck​.​(5A.4) The first substitution is k=y−1xk=y^{-1}xk=y−1x, the second k=z−1yk=z^{-1}yk=z−1y. Theorem 5A.7 (two generating stable copies with an internal flip). Proof. By (5A.9), M~=B(L⊗L⊗ℓ2(Γ))⊗‾RΔ\widetilde M=B(L\otimes L\otimes\ell^2(\Gamma))\overline\otimes R_\DeltaM=B(L⊗L⊗ℓ2(Γ))⊗​RΔ​. Let FLF_LFL​ exchange the two LLL-coordinates and set S=FL⊗JS=F_L\otimes JS=FL​⊗J. Both factors are self-adjoint unitaries of square one, on distinct coordinates. The operator Z~=1L⊗1L⊗Z\widetilde Z=1_L\otimes1_L\otimes ZZ=1L​⊗1L​⊗Z belongs to P′∩M~P'\cap\widetilde MP′∩M. Conjugation by SSS proves strictness in the reverse direction.

5B. Why closing the relative commutants does not repair this pair

Keep exactly the groups, quotient, representation and operators of Section 5A. The question here is whether replacing a copy by its full relative commutant repairs that construction. The product-group argument below supplies the complete commutant calculation without assuming a general tensor-intersection theorem.

Write LG={λg:g∈G}′′\mathcal L_G=\{\lambda_g:g\in G\}''LG​={λg​:g∈G}′′, and take all unqualified commutants in B(V)B(\mathcal V)B(V). Here DDD denotes the second enlarged algebra; the earlier untwisting unitary in (5A.8) is not used in this section.

For completeness, the product group has infinite conjugacy classes away from the identity. 5C. An internal flip forces infinite trace on every product projection

There is a necessary condition on any proposed generating pair in a sigma-finite type II∞\mathrm{II}_\inftyII∞​ factor. A projection finite in one copy need not have finite trace in the containing factor. In fact, an internal symmetry exchanging the copies forces every nonzero product of their projections to have infinite ambient trace. This excludes attempts that begin by normalizing the ambient trace on such a product.

Throughout this section, τM\tau_MτM​ is a faithful normal semifinite trace on a sigma-finite type II∞\mathrm{II}_\inftyII∞​ factor MMM. Finite normal trace existence and uniqueness on finite factors are the exact programme inputs in Traces on von Neumann algebras, Theorems 5.2, 5.5 and 5.9. Equivalence of infinite projections in a sigma-finite factor is the programme Projections and types of von Neumann algebras, Proposition 15.2. Spectral calculus, polar decomposition, central support, the double commutant theorem and Kaplansky density are foundational inputs. We prove the Haar-unitary construction, the finite tensor obstruction and the passage from a finite product corner below. No solidity, primeness or Cartan classification theorem is used.

Hence hnh_nhn​ converges in norm to hhh, with 0≤h−hn≤2−n10\le h-h_n\le2^{-n}10≤h−hn​≤2−n1. Lemma 5C.3 (a finite trace makes commuting factors a spatial product). Suppose F=A∨BF=A\vee BF=A∨B has a faithful normal tracial state ttt, and A,BA,BA,B are commuting unital finite factors. Thus multiplication preserves the product L2L^2L2-inner product on algebraic tensor sums. It extends to an isometry V:L2(A,tA)⊗L2(B,tB)⟶L2(F,t). V:L^2(A,t_A)\otimes L^2(B,t_B)\longrightarrow L^2(F,t). V:L2(A,tA​)⊗L2(B,tB​)⟶L2(F,t). Theorem 5C.4 (infinite ambient trace on every product projection). Let P,Q⊂MP,Q\subset MP,Q⊂M be commuting unital type II∞\mathrm{II}_\inftyII∞​ factors with P∨Q=M,S∈M,S=S∗,S2=1,SPS=Q.(5C.11) P\vee Q=M,\qquad S\in M,\quad S=S^*,\quad S^2=1, \quad SPS=Q. \tag{5C.11} P∨Q=M,S∈M,S=S∗,S2=1,SPS=Q.(5C.11) Then, for every pair of nonzero projections p∈Pp\in Pp∈P, q∈Qq\in Qq∈Q, pq≠0,τM(pq)=∞.(5C.12) pq\ne0,\qquad \tau_M(pq)=\infty. \tag{5C.12} pq=0,τM​(pq)=∞.(5C.12) Mutual relative-commutant equality is not needed for this necessary condition.

5D. A generating internally flipped pair has no normal product state or expectation

The trace obstruction also rules out an expected inclusion. The point is normality: a normal state that factorizes across two commuting factors gives their actual spatial tensor product. For diffuse semifinite copies an internal flip cannot live in that product. This argument applies to the finite-level pair of Section 5A as well as its whole-factor copies; it does not need mutual relative-commutant equality.

We use the bounded GNS construction, ultraweakly closed ideals and weak compactness of a von Neumann algebra's unit ball as foundational inputs, alongside the spatial tensor product and Kaplansky density already used in Section 5C. We prove normality and faithfulness of the representations needed here rather than assuming the state is faithful. The finite-corner contradiction is the complete Lemma 5C.2.

Lemma 5D.1 (a normal state gives a normal faithful representation of a factor). Let FFF be a von Neumann factor and ω\omegaω a normal state. Its GNS representation λω:F→B(Hω)\lambda_\omega:F\to B(H_\omega)λω​:F→B(Hω​) is normal and faithful, even when ω\omegaω is not faithful as a functional. Its image is a von Neumann algebra.

Proof. Write [x][x][x] for the GNS vector of xxx, with ⟨[x],[y]⟩=ω(x∗y)\langle[x],[y]\rangle=\omega(x^*y)⟨[x],[y]⟩=ω(x∗y). Left multiplication is bounded because ∥[ax]∥2≤∥a∥2ω(x∗x).(5D.1) \|[ax]\|^2\le\|a\|^2\omega(x^*x). \tag{5D.1} ∥[ax]∥2≤∥a∥2ω(x∗x).(5D.1) For a bounded increasing net 0≤ai↑a0\le a_i\uparrow a0≤ai​↑a in FFF, normality gives ⟨[x],λω(ai)[x]⟩=ω(x∗aix)↑ω(x∗ax).(5D.2) \langle[x],\lambda_\omega(a_i)[x]\rangle =\omega(x^*a_i x)\uparrow\omega(x^*ax). \tag{5D.2} ⟨[x],λω​(ai​)[x]⟩=ω(x∗ai​x)↑ω(x∗ax).(5D.2) The uniform bound and density of these vectors extend this equality to every vector. Thus the supremum of the represented positive net is λω(a)\lambda_\omega(a)λω​(a), proving normality. The kernel is consequently an ultraweakly closed two-sided ideal, so equals FzFzFz for a central projection zzz. Factoriality and λω(1)=1≠0\lambda_\omega(1)=1\ne0λω​(1)=1=0 force z=0z=0z=0.

A faithful star representation is isometric. Its unit-ball image is ultraweakly compact: it is the image of the ultraweakly compact unit ball of FFF under the normal representation. Kaplansky density then shows that the unit ball of its bicommutant is already this image. Hence the image is weakly closed. A nonfaithful state may have [x]=0[x]=0[x]=0 for a nonzero xxx; faithfulness of the representation says that λω(x)\lambda_\omega(x)λω​(x) is not the zero operator on all GNS vectors. These are different assertions. □\square□

5E. Every normal spatial state is separated from the internally flipped join

Section 5D excludes normal product states. There is a stronger representation statement: allowing an entangled normal state on the spatial tensor product cannot repair the multiplication map. This distinguishes normality of each separate copy from normality on their spatial tensor product. We use the complete factor-GNS proof of Lemma 5D.1, the finite-corner flip obstruction of Proposition 5D.3, and the usual fact that the spatial tensor product of two factors is a factor. No maximal tensor norm or classification of correspondences is needed.

Lemma 5E.1 (agreement of normal states forces the spatial multiplication map). Let P,QP,QP,Q be commuting unital von Neumann factors and M=P∨QM=P\vee QM=P∨Q a factor. Put N=P⊗‾QN=P\overline\otimes QN=P⊗​Q. Suppose ψ\psiψ is a normal state on MMM, Ω\OmegaΩ is a normal state on NNN, and Ω(a⊗b)=ψ(ab),a∈P, b∈Q.(5E.1) \Omega(a\otimes b)=\psi(ab),\qquad a\in P,\ b\in Q. \tag{5E.1} Ω(a⊗b)=ψ(ab),a∈P, b∈Q.(5E.1) Then multiplication extends to a normal isomorphism N→MN\to MN→M. Neither state is assumed faithful, and Ω\OmegaΩ need not be a product state.

Proof. Write λΩ,λψ\lambda_\Omega,\lambda_\psiλΩ​,λψ​ for the two GNS representations. Both are faithful and normal with von Neumann algebra images by Lemma 5D.1. On the span of algebraic tensor GNS vectors, define V[∑iai⊗bi]Ω=[∑iaibi]ψ.(5E.2) V\left[\sum_i a_i\otimes b_i\right]_\Omega =\left[\sum_i a_i b_i\right]_\psi. \tag{5E.2} V[i∑​ai​⊗bi​]Ω​=[i∑​ai​bi​]ψ​.(5E.2) For two such sums the inner products agree, because each cross term satisfies Ω(ai∗aj⊗bi∗bj)=ψ(ai∗ajbi∗bj)=ψ((aibi)∗ajbj).(5E.3) \begin{aligned} \Omega(a_i^*a_j\otimes b_i^*b_j) &=\psi(a_i^*a_j b_i^*b_j)\\ &=\psi((a_i b_i)^*a_j b_j). \end{aligned} \tag{5E.3} Ω(ai∗​aj​⊗bi∗​bj​)​=ψ(ai∗​aj​bi∗​bj​)=ψ((ai​bi​)∗aj​bj​).​(5E.3) Thus the map is well defined on the GNS quotient and is isometric. The algebraic tensors generate NNN; products ababab span a unital star algebra generating MMM. Kaplansky density and normality of the GNS representations therefore make both sets of displayed vectors dense. Explicitly, bounded strong approximations in each represented algebra converge on its cyclic vector, and elements of the norm closure can first be approximated in norm by the indicated spans. Hence VVV extends to a unitary. Left multiplication on these vectors gives VλΩ(a⊗b)V∗=λψ(ab).(5E.4) V\lambda_\Omega(a\otimes b)V^*=\lambda_\psi(ab). \tag{5E.4} VλΩ​(a⊗b)V∗=λψ​(ab).(5E.4) Taking von Neumann closures identifies the two faithful normal images. Their inverse representations are normal: a faithful normal representation is an order isomorphism onto its von Neumann image, so it preserves suprema of bounded increasing positive nets in both directions. This gives the asserted normal multiplication isomorphism. The proof used the cross-term agreement (5E.3), not factorization of Ω\OmegaΩ. □\square□

Theorem 5E.2 (no normal spatial state agrees with the internally flipped join). Suppose P,QP,QP,Q are commuting unital semifinite type II factors, M=P∨QM=P\vee QM=P∨Q is a factor, and S=S∗∈MS=S^*\in MS=S∗∈M, S2=1S^2=1S2=1, exchanges PPP and QQQ. No normal states ψ\psiψ on MMM and Ω\OmegaΩ on P⊗‾QP\overline\otimes QP⊗​Q satisfy (5E.1).

Proof. Such agreement would give the isomorphism of Lemma 5E.1. Transporting SSS into the spatial product would give a self-adjoint unitary implementing the flip through α=Ad⁡S∣P:P→Q\alpha=\operatorname{Ad}S|_P:P\to Qα=AdS∣P​:P→Q. Proposition 5D.3 excludes that unitary by compressing to the diffuse finite corner. □\square□

There is also no nonzero bounded intertwiner between the actual normal representation and a normal spatial tensor representation. This rules out attempts to retain only a common reducing piece rather than matching whole representations.

Proposition 5E.3 (the two normal representations have no common piece). Under the hypotheses of Theorem 5E.2, let π:M→B(H)\pi:M\to B(\mathcal H)π:M→B(H) and θ:N→B(K)\theta:N\to B(\mathcal K)θ:N→B(K) be nonzero unital normal representations, with N=P⊗‾QN=P\overline\otimes QN=P⊗​Q. If a bounded operator T:K→HT:\mathcal K\to\mathcal HT:K→H satisfies Tθ(a⊗b)=π(ab)T(a∈P, b∈Q),(5E.5) T\theta(a\otimes b)=\pi(ab)T\qquad(a\in P,\ b\in Q), \tag{5E.5} Tθ(a⊗b)=π(ab)T(a∈P, b∈Q),(5E.5) then T=0T=0T=0.

Proof. Applying (5E.5) also to adjoints gives T∗T∈θ(N)′T^*T\in\theta(N)'T∗T∈θ(N)′ and TT∗∈π(M)′TT^*\in\pi(M)'TT∗∈π(M)′, first on the generators and then on their von Neumann closures. In the polar decomposition T=U∣T∣T=U|T|T=U∣T∣, its support projections consequently satisfy e=supp⁡∣T∣∈θ(N)′,f=supp⁡∣T∗∣∈π(M)′.(5E.6) \begin{aligned} e&=\operatorname{supp}|T|\in\theta(N)',\\ f&=\operatorname{supp}|T^*|\in\pi(M)'. \end{aligned} \tag{5E.6} ef​=supp∣T∣∈θ(N)′,=supp∣T∗∣∈π(M)′.​(5E.6) If T≠0T\ne0T=0, both are nonzero. Polar decomposition gives a unitary U:eK→fHU:e\mathcal K\to f\mathcal HU:eK→fH. Since ∣T∣|T|∣T∣ commutes with the spatial representation, (5E.5) implies that UUU intertwines its restriction with the actual representation on these subspaces. One may verify this first on the dense range of ∣T∣|T|∣T∣ in eKe\mathcal KeK, then extend by continuity.

Each restricted representation is normal and unital on its nonzero reducing subspace. Its kernel is an ultraweakly closed ideal of a factor, so is zero by the same central-ideal argument as Lemma 5D.1. The unit-ball compactness argument of that lemma also shows that the images are von Neumann algebras. Joint generation now makes their entire images unitarily conjugate. As in Lemma 5E.1, this yields a normal multiplication isomorphism N→MN\to MN→M. Proposition 5D.3 excludes the transported internal flip. Thus the proposed nonzero TTT cannot exist. □\square□

The conclusions concern normal spatial tensor states and representations. They assert neither the absence of arbitrary separately normal algebraic functionals nor a classification of all nonspatial factor representations. In particular, they do not identify MMM with its spatial tensor square or refute the source's unrestricted existence of some different full pair. A candidate pair satisfying all source clauses must be constructed in an actual nonspatial position, and its mutual relative commutants must still be calculated there. Exercise 6.21 shows why keeping the internal flip while dropping joint generation defeats this obstruction.

5F. The one-sided repair still has no internal exchange after stabilization

Proposition 5B.2 distinguishes the ambient commutants of the finite-level pair by finiteness. That distinction disappears after both copies receive an infinite matrix coordinate. A different obstruction survives: an internal unitary fixes the ambient commutant pointwise, and would transfer a normal conditional expectation to a position where normality is impossible. The proof below excludes this particular stabilized repair without assuming that its two factors are isomorphic to the whole ambient factor.

5G. A finite factor forbids a normal expectation in every represented position

The regular-basis proof in Lemma 5F.1 uses the group translations to assign equal state mass to all rank-one basis projections. For an infinite-dimensional finite factor, a trace-class density gives an obstruction in any normal unital representation, including a representation on a nonseparable Hilbert space. Combining this fact with Lemma 5F.2 yields a test for internal conjugacy whose hypotheses specify the actual outside algebra and its embedding.

Lemma 5G.1 (no normal expectation onto an infinite-dimensional finite factor). Let N0⊂B(K)N_0\subset B(K)N0​⊂B(K) be an infinite-dimensional finite factor, represented normally and unitally, and let τ\tauτ be its normalized faithful normal trace. There is no normal conditional expectation F:B(K)⟶N0.(5G.1) F:B(K)\longrightarrow N_0. \tag{5G.1} F:B(K)⟶N0​.(5G.1) No faithfulness assumption on FFF, and no separability assumption on KKK, is required.

Proof. Suppose that FFF exists. The functional ω=τ∘F\omega=\tau\circ Fω=τ∘F is a normal state on B(K)B(K)B(K). The normal-functional/trace-class correspondence gives a positive trace-class operator ddd such that ω(X)=Tr⁡K(dX),Tr⁡K(d)=1.(5G.2) \omega(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_K(dX),\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_K(d)=1. \tag{5G.2} ω(X)=TrK​(dX),TrK​(d)=1.(5G.2) This correspondence holds on an arbitrary Hilbert space. For every unitary u∈N0u\in N_0u∈N0​, bimodularity of FFF and traciality of τ\tauτ give ω(uXu∗)=τ(uF(X)u∗)=ω(X),X∈B(K).(5G.3) \begin{aligned} \omega(uXu^*)&=\tau\bigl(uF(X)u^*\bigr)\\ &=\omega(X),\qquad X\in B(K). \end{aligned} \tag{5G.3} ω(uXu∗)​=τ(uF(X)u∗)=ω(X),X∈B(K).​(5G.3) By cyclicity of the trace-class pairing, this says Tr⁡K((u∗du−d)X)=0\operatorname{Tr}_K((u^*du-d)X)=0TrK​((u∗du−d)X)=0 for every X∈B(K)X\in B(K)X∈B(K). Nondegeneracy of that pairing yields u∗du=du^*du=du∗du=d. Since elements of N0N_0N0​ are linear combinations of its unitaries, d∈N0′d\in N_0'd∈N0′​.

The operator ddd is nonzero, positive and compact. The compact spectral theorem supplies a positive eigenvalue μ>0\mu>0μ>0 whose eigenspace KμK_\muKμ​ is nonzero and finite-dimensional. Its spectral projection eμ=1{μ}(d)e_\mu=1_{\{\mu\}}(d)eμ​=1{μ}​(d) commutes with N0N_0N0​. Thus KμK_\muKμ​ reduces N0N_0N0​, and restriction defines a normal unital representation πμ:N0⟶B(Kμ),πμ(n)=n∣Kμ.(5G.4) \pi_\mu:N_0\longrightarrow B(K_\mu),\qquad \pi_\mu(n)=n|_{K_\mu}. \tag{5G.4} πμ​:N0​⟶B(Kμ​),πμ​(n)=n∣Kμ​​.(5G.4) Normality follows from normality of the original representation and compression to the reducing subspace. The kernel is an ultraweakly closed two-sided ideal, hence ker⁡πμ=N0z\ker\pi_\mu=N_0zkerπμ​=N0​z for a central projection z∈N0z\in N_0z∈N0​. Factoriality makes zzz either zero or one. Since πμ(1)=1Kμ≠0\pi_\mu(1)=1_{K_\mu}\ne0πμ​(1)=1Kμ​​=0, the kernel is zero. This injects the infinite-dimensional vector space N0N_0N0​ into the finite-dimensional algebra B(Kμ)B(K_\mu)B(Kμ​), a contradiction. □\square□

The operator-algebra inputs in this proof are the trace on a finite factor, the trace-class description of normal functionals on B(K)B(K)B(K), the compact spectral theorem, and the central-projection description of ultraweakly closed ideals. No group action, amenability or transitive rank-one basis is used. Exercise 6.24 shows why finite-dimensional factors form a real boundary; Exercise 6.25 isolates the trace-class mechanism without a state normalization.

Its range lies in N0N_0N0​, and F0(n)=nF_0(n)=nF0​(n)=n for n∈N0n\in N_0n∈N0​, so it is a projection onto that algebra. 5H. Matrix coordinates preserve the infinite-trace obstruction

The source problem concerns two copies of the entire properly infinite factor, in their actual represented positions. Selecting the source’s rank-one matrix corner inside each copy recovers two copies of its specified finite group factor. The simultaneous matrix coordinates recover all the original source clauses, but their coefficient algebra has infinite ambient trace. We prove both directions of this reduction and then show that, in the notation defined below, compression by every projection 0≠h≤r0\ne h\le r0=h≤r with T(h)<∞T(h)<\inftyT(h)<∞ loses multiplicativity on each coefficient copy.

Fix the normal identification supplied by Sections 4 and 5A, L=ℓ2(N),N=L(F∞),M=B(L)⊗‾N,T=Tr⁡L⊗τN.(5H.1) \begin{gathered} L=\ell^2(\mathbb N),\qquad N=L(F_\infty),\\ M=B(L)\overline\otimes N,\\ T=\operatorname{Tr}_L\otimes\tau_N. \end{gathered} \tag{5H.1} L=ℓ2(N),N=L(F∞​),M=B(L)⊗​N,T=TrL​⊗τN​.​(5H.1) Here F∞F_\inftyF∞​ is the free group on countably many generators, and τN\tau_NτN​ is its normalized group trace. The inversion unitary in Lemma 5A.3 normally identifies the course's right regular factor with this left regular factor. We select the rank-one matrix corner of this very NNN; we assume no isomorphism between unspecified finite amplifications of group factors.

The trace input is the fully proved Theorem 5C.4, with precisely the finite-trace and projection-comparison prerequisites declared in Section 5C. We use the finite-normal-trace existence input already declared there, together with the complete Lemmas 5C.2–5C.3, to identify the corner's type. The additional foundational inputs are matrix units, normal representations and their ultraweakly closed central ideals, ultraweak unit-ball compactness and Kaplansky density as in Lemma 5D.1, nonzero corners of factors, Hilbert space direct sums, strong operator limits, the spatial tensor product, and the double commutant theorem. The matrix, corner-trace and compression arguments are proved below. No solidity theorem, classification of free-group factors, or normal spatial multiplication map for the two coefficient copies is an input.

Theorem 5H.1 (exact simultaneous matrix reduction and its whole-copy converse). Suppose a normal unital endomorphism σ:M→M\sigma:M\to Mσ:M→M and an internal self-adjoint unitary S∈MS\in MS∈M, S2=1S^2=1S2=1, satisfy P=σ(M),Q=SPS,[P,Q]=0,P′∩M=Q,Q′∩M=P,P∨Q=M.(5H.2) \begin{gathered} P=\sigma(M),\qquad Q=SPS,\qquad [P,Q]=0,\\ P'\cap M=Q,\qquad Q'\cap M=P,\\ P\vee Q=M. \end{gathered} \tag{5H.2} P=σ(M),Q=SPS,[P,Q]=0,P′∩M=Q,Q′∩M=P,P∨Q=M.​(5H.2) Let EijE_{ij}Eij​ be the usual matrix units of B(L)B(L)B(L), and put eij=σ(Eij⊗1N),fij=SeijS,p=e11,q=f11,r=pq.(5H.3) \begin{gathered} e_{ij}=\sigma(E_{ij}\otimes1_N),\\ f_{ij}=Se_{ij}S,\\ p=e_{11},\quad q=f_{11},\quad r=pq. \end{gathered} \tag{5H.3} eij​=σ(Eij​⊗1N​),fij​=Seij​S,p=e11​,q=f11​,r=pq.​(5H.3) Then 0≠r,T(r)=∞,SrS=r.(5H.4) 0\ne r,\qquad T(r)=\infty,\qquad SrS=r. \tag{5H.4} 0=r,T(r)=∞,SrS=r.(5H.4) The corner R=rMrR=rMrR=rMr, with identity rrr, is a sigma-finite type II∞\mathrm{II}_\inftyII∞​ factor. In particular s=s∗s=s^*s=s∗, s2=rs^2=rs2=r, and sAs=BsAs=BsAs=B.

Conversely, suppose a sigma-finite factor RRR, with identity 1R1_R1R​, contains commuting normal unital copies A,BA,BA,B of this same NNN, satisfies (5H.6), and has a self-adjoint unitary s∈Rs\in Rs∈R with s2=1Rs^2=1_Rs2=1R​, sAs=BsAs=BsAs=B. Suppose also that a normal ambient isomorphism is supplied: Θ:B(L)⊗‾B(L)⊗‾R⟶M.(5H.9) \Theta:B(L)\overline\otimes B(L)\overline\otimes R \longrightarrow M. \tag{5H.9} Θ:B(L)⊗​B(L)⊗​R⟶M.(5H.9) Then these data produce a normal unital endomorphism σ\sigmaσ and an internal SSS satisfying every clause of (5H.2). Thus existence of a whole-copy source pair in this MMM is equivalent to existence of these reduced data including Θ\ThetaΘ.

Proof. The kernel of σ\sigmaσ is an ultraweakly closed two-sided ideal in the factor MMM, hence is zero or all of MMM. Unitality rules out the latter. Thus σ\sigmaσ is injective, and P,QP,QP,Q are normal copies of the entire type II∞\mathrm{II}_\inftyII∞​ factor. A faithful normal homomorphism is a normal isomorphism onto its image: its isometry carries the ultraweakly compact unit ball onto the image unit ball, making the latter weakly closed, and preservation of increasing positive suprema gives normality of the inverse. This is also the unit-ball argument used in Lemma 5D.1.

Normality gives ∑ieii=1\sum_i e_{ii}=1∑i​eii​=1 strongly; conjugation gives ∑kfkk=1\sum_k f_{kk}=1∑k​fkk​=1 strongly. The two matrix-unit families commute because the whole algebras P,QP,QP,Q do. Conjugation by SSS interchanges the families, so SpS=qSpS=qSpS=q, SqS=pSqS=pSqS=p, and SrS=qp=rSrS=qp=rSrS=qp=r. Theorem 5C.4 applied to the nonzero projections p∈Pp\in Pp∈P, q∈Qq\in Qq∈Q gives the other two assertions of (5H.4). These conclusions hold in every faithful normal realization; the theorem concerns the actual ambient trace, not a trace in either copy.

The source corner (E11⊗1N)M(E11⊗1N)(E_{11}\otimes1_N)M(E_{11}\otimes1_N)(E11​⊗1N​)M(E11​⊗1N​) is normally isomorphic to NNN. Consequently pPp≅NpPp\cong NpPp≅N normally, and qQq≅NqQq\cong NqQq≅N by conjugation. For a∈pPpa\in pPpa∈pPp, aaa commutes with qqq, so a↦aqa\mapsto aqa↦aq is a normal star homomorphism into rMrrMrrMr, with unit image rrr. Its kernel is a central ideal of the factor pPppPppPp, and r≠0r\ne0r=0; therefore it is injective. Its image is a von Neumann algebra by the same normal unit-ball argument. The identical argument for b↦pbb\mapsto pbb↦pb proves that A,BA,BA,B in (5H.5) are normal unital copies of precisely NNN. They commute because their preimages belong to the commuting P,QP,QP,Q.

The trace T∣RT|_RT∣R​ is faithful, normal and semifinite. To see semifiniteness directly, for a nonzero positive x∈rMrx\in rMrx∈rMr choose a nonzero positive y≤xy\le xy≤x of finite TTT-trace in MMM; positivity and x=rxrx=rxrx=rxr force y=ryry=ryry=ryr. A nonzero corner of a factor is a factor. If ϕ\phiϕ is a faithful normal state on the sigma-finite MMM, then ϕ(r)>0\phi(r)>0ϕ(r)>0 and y↦ϕ(y)/ϕ(r)y\mapsto\phi(y)/\phi(r)y↦ϕ(y)/ϕ(r) is a faithful normal state on RRR, proving its sigma-finiteness. For any projection e≤re\le re≤r, eRe=eMeeRe=eMeeRe=eMe. Thus a nonzero minimal projection of RRR would also be minimal in MMM, which has none. We will exclude finiteness of RRR below after proving its join and internal symmetry.

Since P∨Q=MP\vee Q=MP∨Q=M, compressing this equality at E11⊗E11⊗rE_{11}\otimes E_{11}\otimes rE11​⊗E11​⊗r gives A∨B=RA\vee B=RA∨B=R.

We spell out the relative-commutant calculation to preserve both source clauses. An operator in the ambient tensor algebra commuting with all Eij⊗1L⊗rE_{ij}\otimes1_L\otimes rEij​⊗1L​⊗r has vanishing off-diagonal first-coordinate blocks and identical diagonal blocks. Finite second-coordinate compressions, followed by their strong limit, prove U∗(P′∩M)U=1L⊗‾B(L)⊗‾(A′∩R),U∗(Q′∩M)U=B(L)⊗‾1L⊗‾(B′∩R).(5H.15) \begin{aligned} U^*(P'\cap M)U &=1_L\overline\otimes B(L)\overline\otimes(A'\cap R),\\ U^*(Q'\cap M)U &=B(L)\overline\otimes1_L\overline\otimes(B'\cap R). \end{aligned} \tag{5H.15} U∗(P′∩M)UU∗(Q′∩M)U​=1L​⊗​B(L)⊗​(A′∩R),=B(L)⊗​1L​⊗​(B′∩R).​(5H.15) The reverse inclusions follow directly by multiplication. Because SSS commutes with rrr, the actual corner operator s=rSrs=rSrs=rSr is self-adjoint and satisfies s2=rs^2=rs2=r. It is therefore a unitary for RRR's identity. If a∈pPpa\in pPpa∈pPp, then s(aq)s=p(SaS)∈B, s(aq)s=p(SaS)\in B, s(aq)s=p(SaS)∈B, and conjugation in the other direction gives sAs=BsAs=BsAs=B. Moreover SuikS=ukiS u_{ik}S=u_{ki}Suik​S=uki​. If RRR were finite, the finite-normal-trace existence input of Section 5C would supply a faithful normal tracial state on it. Since the finite factors A,BA,BA,B commute and generate RRR, Lemma 5C.3 would make multiplication a normal spatial isomorphism A⊗‾B→RA\overline\otimes B\to RA⊗​B→R. V(a\otimes1_A)V=1_A\otimes a\qquad(a\in A). V(a⊗1A​)V=1A​⊗a(a∈A). This contradicts the complete finite tensor-flip obstruction of Lemma 5C.2, since A≅NA\cong NA≅N is diffuse. Thus RRR is not finite. It is a semifinite factor without nonzero minimal projections, so it is type II∞\mathrm{II}_\inftyII∞​. This establishes the type using the existing finite-trace and finite-flip package; the separate ambient-trace identity T(r)=∞T(r)=\inftyT(r)=∞ remains the direct conclusion of Theorem 5C.4. Finally the inverse of x↦U∗xUx\mapsto U^*xUx↦U∗xU is a normal ambient isomorphism of the form (5H.9), proving the necessity of Θ\ThetaΘ.

For the converse, set D=B(L)⊗‾B(L)⊗‾R,P=B(L)⊗‾1L⊗‾A,Q=1L⊗‾B(L)⊗‾B,S0=FL⊗s.(5H.16) \begin{aligned} \mathcal D&=B(L)\overline\otimes B(L)\overline\otimes R,\\ \mathcal P&=B(L)\overline\otimes1_L\overline\otimes A,\qquad \mathcal Q=1_L\overline\otimes B(L)\overline\otimes B,\\ S_0&=F_L\otimes s. \end{aligned} \tag{5H.16} DPS0​​=B(L)⊗​B(L)⊗​R,=B(L)⊗​1L​⊗​A,Q=1L​⊗​B(L)⊗​B,=FL​⊗s.​(5H.16) The flip FLF_LFL​ belongs to B(L⊗L)=B(L)⊗‾B(L)B(L\otimes L)=B(L)\overline\otimes B(L)B(L⊗L)=B(L)⊗​B(L); finite matrix corners verify the latter equality by the same coefficient argument. Thus S0S_0S0​ is internal to D\mathcal DD, self-adjoint and of square one, and it exchanges P,Q\mathcal P,\mathcal QP,Q. They commute. Their join is D\mathcal DD because A∨B=RA\vee B=RA∨B=R. The matrix-unit proof of (5H.15), now inside D\mathcal DD, and the two assumed relative commutants give P′∩D=Q\mathcal P'\cap\mathcal D=\mathcal QP′∩D=Q and Q′∩D=P\mathcal Q'\cap\mathcal D=\mathcal PQ′∩D=P.

Choose a normal unital isomorphism α:N→A\alpha:N\to Aα:N→A, as guaranteed by the specified copy assumption. The map ψ:M⟶P,ψ(Eij⊗n)=Eij⊗1L⊗α(n) \begin{gathered} \psi:M\longrightarrow\mathcal P,\\ \psi(E_{ij}\otimes n)\\ =E_{ij}\otimes1_L\otimes\alpha(n) \end{gathered} ψ:M⟶P,ψ(Eij​⊗n)=Eij​⊗1L​⊗α(n)​ extends normally to an onto unital isomorphism. Applying Θ\ThetaΘ to the commutation, join, two relative commutants and involution identities proves every clause of (5H.2). In particular the domain and ambient codomain of σ\sigmaσ are the same whole MMM. Without Θ\ThetaΘ, the displayed construction gives a map into D\mathcal DD, and has not given an endomorphism of MMM. □\square□

Proposition 5H.2 (finite compression obstruction inside the coefficient corner). In the forward reduction of Theorem 5H.1, let TR=T∣RT_R=T|_RTR​=T∣R​. For every projection 0≠h≤r0\ne h\le r0=h≤r with TR(h)<∞T_R(h)<\inftyTR​(h)<∞, hhh commutes with neither whole algebra, and neither of the normal compression maps ch:A⟶hRh,a⟼hah,ch:B⟶hRh,b⟼hbh(5H.17) \begin{gathered} c_h:A\longrightarrow hRh,\quad a\longmapsto hah,\\ c_h:B\longrightarrow hRh,\quad b\longmapsto hbh \end{gathered} \tag{5H.17} ch​:A⟶hRh,a⟼hah,ch​:B⟶hRh,b⟼hbh​(5H.17) is multiplicative. Proof. By the isomorphisms in (5H.5), every nonzero projection z∈Az\in Az∈A is a0qa_0qa0​q for a nonzero projection a0∈pPpa_0\in pPpa0​∈pPp, and every nonzero projection z∈Bz\in Bz∈B is pb0pb_0pb0​ for a nonzero projection b0∈qQqb_0\in qQqb0​∈qQq. Injectivity shows that the preimages are projections, and that they are nonzero. Theorem 5C.4 therefore gives TR(z)=∞(0≠z∈Proj⁡(A)∪Proj⁡(B)).(5H.20) \begin{gathered} T_R(z)=\infty\\ \bigl(0\ne z\in\operatorname{Proj}(A)\cup\operatorname{Proj}(B)\bigr). \end{gathered} \tag{5H.20} TR​(z)=∞(0=z∈Proj(A)∪Proj(B)).​(5H.20) If a nonzero finite-TRT_RTR​ projection hhh commuted with all of AAA, then h∈A′∩R=Bh\in A'\cap R=Bh∈A′∩R=B by (5H.6), contradicting (5H.20). If it commuted with all of BBB, the other relative commutant would similarly place it in AAA. This proves the two noncommutation statements for every such hhh, with no special choice of its represented form.

For any unital star algebra D⊂RD\subset RD⊂R, multiplication directly gives (5H.18) for every x∈Dx\in Dx∈D. Suppose ch∣Dc_h|_Dch​∣D​ is multiplicative. The defect then vanishes for all x∈Dx\in Dx∈D, so (r−h)xh=0(r-h)xh=0(r−h)xh=0 for all xxx. Apply this conclusion to x∗x^*x∗ and take adjoints to obtain hx(r−h)=0hx(r-h)=0hx(r−h)=0. Since rrr is the identity of DDD, these two equalities give xh=hxh=hxxh=hxh=hxxh=hxh=hx. Conversely, if hhh commutes with every x∈Dx\in Dx∈D, then (hxh)(hyh)=hxyh(x,y∈D), (hxh)(hyh)=hxyh\qquad(x,y\in D), (hxh)(hyh)=hxyh(x,y∈D), so the compression is multiplicative. We have proved the exact equivalence ch∣D is a homomorphism⟺h∈D′∩R.(5H.21) \begin{gathered} c_h|_D\text{ is a homomorphism}\\ \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h\in D'\cap R. \end{gathered} \tag{5H.21} ch​∣D​ is a homomorphism⟺h∈D′∩R.​(5H.21) For D=AD=AD=A and for D=BD=BD=B, noncommutation provides an element whose real or imaginary part is a self-adjoint x∈Dx\in Dx∈D with [h,x]≠0[h,x]\ne0[h,x]=0. For self-adjoint xxx, the two off-diagonal blocks (r−h)xh(r-h)xh(r−h)xh and hx(r−h)hx(r-h)hx(r−h) are adjoints. Thus [h,x]≠0[h,x]\ne0[h,x]=0 forces (r−h)xh≠0(r-h)xh\ne0(r−h)xh=0, and (5H.18) is strictly nonzero and positive. This proves the advertised failure, with an actual defect in each copy rather than only a failure of a proposed normalization.

For the converse, use σ,S\sigma,Sσ,S constructed in Theorem 5H.1. Its selected projections are p=Θ(E11⊗1L⊗1R)p=\Theta(E_{11}\otimes1_L\otimes1_R)p=Θ(E11​⊗1L​⊗1R​), q=Θ(1L⊗E11⊗1R)q=\Theta(1_L\otimes E_{11}\otimes1_R)q=Θ(1L​⊗E11​⊗1R​), and their product is r0=Θ(E11⊗E11⊗1R)r_0=\Theta(E_{11}\otimes E_{11}\otimes1_R)r0​=Θ(E11​⊗E11​⊗1R​). The map y↦Θ(E11⊗E11⊗y)y\mapsto\Theta(E_{11}\otimes E_{11}\otimes y)y↦Θ(E11​⊗E11​⊗y) is a normal isomorphism of RRR onto r0Mr0r_0Mr_0r0​Mr0​, carrying A,BA,BA,B to the forward reduced copies. Pulling the faithful normal semifinite corner trace back gives exactly (5H.19). The assertions just proved transport through this isomorphism. □\square□

These statements identify the finite-corner obstruction exactly. The intrinsic units of A,BA,BA,B are finite in those copies, whereas the coefficient identity rrr has infinite ambient trace. Every projection 0≠h≤r0\ne h\le r0=h≤r with TR(h)<∞T_R(h)<\inftyTR​(h)<∞ destroys the multiplication of both prescribed copies. The condition h≤rh\le rh≤r matters: if a projection h∈Mh\in Mh∈M is orthogonal to rrr, then hAh=hBh=0hAh=hBh=0hAh=hBh=0; these are multiplicative zero maps and give no unital copies. A compressed set hAhhAhhAh need not be an algebra, and closing it under multiplication does not make a↦haha\mapsto haha↦hah a homomorphism. Commutation of A,BA,BA,B alone also does not imply commutation of their separately compressed sets when hhh commutes with neither. An explicit finite counterexample appears in Exercise 6.28. A different proposed finite-corner construction would have to supply its own actual normal representations and verify their properties.

The reduced source problem is therefore to produce R,A,B,s,ΘR,A,B,s,\ThetaR,A,B,s,Θ with all the hypotheses of Theorem 5H.1, or to exclude that exact infinite-trace position. The theorem does not construct those data. The normal-expectation exclusion in Theorem 5D.4 also applies to the finite copies A,B⊂RA,B\subset RA,B⊂R, using their join and internal sss; its absence does not settle the source question, which asks for no such expectation. The unrestricted assertion of Connes's Corollary 11 remains open at the present measurable scope. The human source is Connes's author-hosted typeset text, Corollary 11 and the following Sakai note, PDF 44–45. The simultaneous reduction, converse and compression proof here are new original arguments dedicated to CC0; no human proof has been copied into that dedication.

6. Exercises with complete solutions

Level 1 is a direct calculation. Level 2 proves part of the mechanism. Level 3 compares the full hypotheses or combines results.

Exercise 6.1. Level 2. Prove that an ordinary Borel scalar function of a(x)a(x)a(x) is constant. Does passing to the Lebesgue completion change the answer?

Solution. The range of the scalar function on Γ\GammaΓ is countable. If two attained values differ, the inverse image of one value is the union of a nonempty proper collection of the classes AgA_gAg​. Measurability would make that union Borel. Lemma 1.1 forbids it. The same lemma forbids completion-measurability, because both that union and its complement have inner Lebesgue measure zero and cannot be measurable while covering XXX. Thus the answer is unchanged by completion.

Exercise 6.2. Level 1. For Γ=F2\Gamma=F_2Γ=F2​, let F={e,a,b}F=\{e,a,b\}F={e,a,b}, ℓ(B)=2/5\ell(B)=2/5ℓ(B)=2/5, and C=XC=XC=X. Calculate the fibre mass of {s∈B,d∈F}\{s\in B,d\in F\}{s∈B,d∈F}, its mass after any left translation, Λ(ν)\Lambda(\nu)Λ(ν), and Λν(B)\Lambda_\nu(B)Λν​(B).

Solution. Each label has source-BBB mass 2/52/52/5, so the first mass is 6/56/56/5. Left translation changes FFF to a three-element translate and preserves sss, so the mass is again 6/56/56/5. The transverse value is Λ(ν)=1\Lambda(\nu)=1Λ(ν)=1, and the unit value is Λν(B)=2/5\Lambda_\nu(B)=2/5Λν​(B)=2/5. The full fibre mass is infinite. None of these four quantities should be substituted for another.

Exercise 6.3. Level 2. What does this say about source-coordinate density?

Solution. By (2.3) the squared distance is ∫X(∣1−f∣2+∣f∣2) dℓ=2∥f−12∥22+12. \int_X\bigl(|1-f|^2+|f|^2\bigr)\,d\ell =2\|f-\tfrac12\|_2^2+\tfrac12. ∫X​(∣1−f∣2+∣f∣2)dℓ=2∥f−21​∥22​+21​. Its minimum is 1/21/21/2, attained by f=1/2f=1/2f=1/2. Thus even on a finite proper stage the extra relative-label event cannot be approximated by source-coordinate functions. The failure is an L2L^2L2 failure, not just the absence of a pointwise Borel inverse. Normalizing this stage to a probability divides the minimum by two, giving 1/41/41/4.

Exercise 6.4. Level 2. Prove faithfulness and traciality of (4.5) without assuming a group-factor classification theorem.

Solution. For TTT commuting with all λh\lambda_hλh​, its column at hhh is the left translate by hhh of its column c=Tδec=T\delta_ec=Tδe​. Therefore the coefficients of T∗δeT^*\delta_eT∗δe​ are cg−1‾\overline{c_{g^{-1}}}cg−1​​, and their squared sum equals that of ccc. This proves τ(T∗T)=τ(TT∗)\tau(T^*T)=\tau(TT^*)τ(T∗T)=τ(TT∗). Polarization gives the trace identity for all products. If T≥0T\ge0T≥0 has trace zero, then T1/2δe=0T^{1/2}\delta_e=0T1/2δe​=0; commutation gives zero on each δh=λhδe\delta_h=\lambda_h\delta_eδh​=λh​δe​. The square root and hence TTT are zero. Normality is the ordinary vector-functional property, so this is a normal faithful tracial state.

Exercise 6.5. Level 3. Verify the covariance of WhW_hWh​, then use h=ah=ah=a to prove failure of both relative-commutant equality and joint generation.

Solution. Conjugating its kkk-slice by simultaneous left translation replaces that slice with the lklklk-slice and its first translation with λlkhk−1l−1\lambda_{lkhk^{-1}l^{-1}}λlkhk−1l−1​. This is precisely the coefficient assigned to lklklk in (5.3), so the whole unitary is unchanged and belongs to EEE. Its first translations commute with every member of the first RΓR_\GammaRΓ​; its identities on KKK give commutation with the whole PPP. But QQQ and P∨QP\vee QP∨Q commute with the separate first λb\lambda_bλb​, whereas (5.5) gives δba\delta_{ba}δba​ and δab\delta_{ab}δab​. Thus Wa∈P′∩E∖QW_a\in P'\cap E\setminus QWa​∈P′∩E∖Q and Wa∉P∨QW_a\notin P\vee QWa​∈/P∨Q. The flip still exchanges P,QP,QP,Q and squares to one; those properties alone do not prove either of the failed assertions.

Exercise 6.6. Level 3. Which source conclusion has this factor example disproved: existence of some suitable pair in Connes's Corollary 11, or validity of the canonical tensor pair at the weaker measurable scope? Why is it consistent with Claude-SQ's actual Proposition 8.5?

Solution. The explicit unitary disproves the relative-commutant and generation claims for the particular canonical tensor pair at the weaker scope. It does not rule out a different endomorphism and symmetry in MMM, so it does not refute the existential Corollary 11. Claude-SQ states a standard Borel arrow hypothesis for all of Sections 5 and 8, including Proposition 8.5. Our arrow space is not standard Borel by Proposition 2.1. Its proof uses the standard fibre-density Proposition 5.1; Exercise 6.3 shows that the required density is false here.

Exercise 6.7. Level 2. Prove the discrete regular commutation theorem (5A.3) by matrix coefficients. Justify both changes of variable and absolute convergence, rather than assuming that a general convolution operator is a bounded finite-support limit.

Solution. For operators commuting with the left and right translations respectively, the columns at the identity give Tx,z=cz−1xT_{x,z}=c_{z^{-1}x}Tx,z​=cz−1x​ and Ux,z=dxz−1U_{x,z}=d_{xz^{-1}}Ux,z​=dxz−1​. The coefficient of TUTUTU is ∑ycy−1xdyz−1\sum_y c_{y^{-1}x}d_{yz^{-1}}∑y​cy−1x​dyz−1​; set k=y−1xk=y^{-1}xk=y−1x to obtain ∑kckdxk−1z−1\sum_k c_kd_{xk^{-1}z^{-1}}∑k​ck​dxk−1z−1​. The coefficient of UTUTUT is ∑ydxy−1cz−1y\sum_y d_{xy^{-1}}c_{z^{-1}y}∑y​dxy−1​cz−1y​; set k=z−1yk=z^{-1}yk=z−1y to obtain the same sum. Each is bounded absolutely by ∥c∥2∥d∥2\|c\|_2\|d\|_2∥c∥2​∥d∥2​, since the index permutations preserve the squared sums. Thus the operators commute. The left commutant is contained in the double commutant of the right generators; their commutation gives the opposite inclusion. Taking commutants gives the second assertion. □\square□

Exercise 6.8. Level 2. Distinguish π\piπ from β\betaβ in (5A.2), prove the HHH-conjugacy assertion for each nonidentity word, and use it to eliminate all nonscalar coefficients in (5A.5). For w=a1a0w=a_1a_0w=a1​a0​, choose h=a2a0a2−1h=a_2a_0a_2^{-1}h=a2​a0​a2−1​ and compute the lengths of hmwh−mh^mwh^{-m}hmwh−m.

Solution. The map π\piπ is onto because bn=π(an+1)b_n=\pi(a_{n+1})bn​=π(an+1​), and has a0≠ea_0\ne ea0​=e in its kernel. The map β\betaβ bijects the free generating sets, so is an isomorphism and sends a0a_0a0​ to b0≠eb_0\ne eb0​=e. For an arbitrary word choose a generator aja_jaj​ not occurring in it, with j≥1j\ge1j≥1. Then aja0aj−1a_ja_0a_j^{-1}aj​a0​aj−1​ is in HHH, and the displayed conjugates (5A.6) are reduced with distinct lengths 2m+4+∣w∣2m+4+|w|2m+4+∣w∣. If a commuting operator has a coefficient constant on one of these infinite orbits, square summability makes that coefficient zero. Only the identity coefficient survives, and commutation with left translations makes the whole operator scalar. In the requested example ∣w∣=2|w|=2∣w∣=2, so the lengths are 2m+62m+62m+6, namely 8,10,12,…8,10,12,\ldots8,10,12,…. □\square□

Exercise 6.9. Level 3. Prove that BBB is a normal copy using DDD, compute the entire A∨BA\vee BA∨B commutant, and verify J2=1J^2=1J2=1, internality and (5A.12). Explain why this JJJ is not the plain flip of the two Hilbert coordinates.

Solution. The inverse of DDD multiplies the second coordinate on the right by π(x)\pi(x)π(x). Applying a BBB-generator and then DDD leaves it unchanged because π(x)π(g)−1π(xg−1)−1=e\pi(x)\pi(g)^{-1}\pi(xg^{-1})^{-1}=eπ(x)π(g)−1π(xg−1)−1=e. The first coordinate becomes xg−1xg^{-1}xg−1, so DBD∗=RΓ⊗1D B D^*=R_\Gamma\otimes1DBD∗=RΓ​⊗1. A member of (A∨B)′(A\vee B)'(A∨B)′ has first coefficients in RΓR_\GammaRΓ​; the kernel generators force them to be scalar by (5A.5). It is therefore 1⊗C1\otimes C1⊗C, and surjectivity of π\piπ forces CCC to commute with every right translation of Δ\DeltaΔ. The converse is immediate, giving (5A.10) and then (5A.9).

For JJJ, the second application multiplies qπ(x)−1q\pi(x)^{-1}qπ(x)−1 by π(x−1)−1=π(x)\pi(x^{-1})^{-1}=\pi(x)π(x−1)−1=π(x), returning qqq, and restores xxx. It commutes with left multiplication on qqq, so is in the computed generated algebra. Applying JJJ, then λg⊗1\lambda_g\otimes1λg​⊗1, then JJJ, gives (xg−1,qπ(g)−1)(xg^{-1},q\pi(g)^{-1})(xg−1,qπ(g)−1), exactly the BBB-generator. This permutation inverts the first coordinate and modifies the second using the quotient; it does not exchange the two coordinates. □\square□

Exercise 6.10. Level 3. Prove (5A.15), carry the extra unitary through the stabilization, and state precisely which assertions of Connes's Corollary 11 hold for this pair. Does the calculation disprove the existence of a different pair?

Solution. The BBB-generators preserve the graph q=π(x)q=\pi(x)q=π(x) in both directions. Its span is therefore reducing, and its projection commutes with BBB. The identity basis vector lies in that span. Applying 1⊗ρb01\otimes\rho_{b_0}1⊗ρb0​​ gives (e,b0−1)(e,b_0^{-1})(e,b0−1​), which is outside the graph since π(e)=e\pi(e)=eπ(e)=e. Thus Z∈A′∩E∖BZ\in A'\cap E\setminus BZ∈A′∩E∖B. In M~\widetilde MM, tensoring ZZZ with the two LLL-identities gives an element commuting with PPP. Membership in QQQ would, by a unit-vector matrix coefficient in the second LLL-coordinate, imply Z∈BZ\in BZ∈B, a contradiction. The symmetry gives the reverse strict inclusion.

The normal unital endomorphism produces a copy of the whole properly infinite factor, its symmetry is internal and squares to one, the two copies commute, and they jointly generate the entire factor. Each relative commutant is nevertheless strictly larger than the other copy. This pair therefore fails that source clause. The existential conclusion remains open because the argument has not ruled out other endomorphisms and symmetries. □\square□

Exercise 6.11. Level 2. Compute A′∩EA'\cap EA′∩E by applying Lemma 5A.1 to the product group. Explain why finite matrix compressions alone would not justify a general tensor-intersection identity. Then prove C′∩E=AC'\cap E=AC′∩E=A.

Solution. The group Γ×Δ\Gamma\times\DeltaΓ×Δ acts by λg⊗λq\lambda_g\otimes\lambda_qλg​⊗λq​ on the displayed basis. By (5A.10), membership in EEE is commutation with all second left translations, so imposing commutation with AAA imposes exactly all product left translations. Lemma 5A.1 gives the algebra of product right translations, which is RΓ⊗‾RΔ=CR_\Gamma\overline\otimes R_\Delta=CRΓ​⊗​RΔ​=C. A finite projection onto second-coordinate basis vectors need not belong to RΔR_\DeltaRΔ​. Compressing by it therefore need not retain a proposed tensor algebra with that restricted second factor; the product-group argument avoids this gap. To compute C′∩EC'\cap EC′∩E, its first-coordinate matrix coefficients belong to RΔR_\DeltaRΔ​ and commute with RΔR_\DeltaRΔ​. The scalar centre makes them scalar, hence the operator is T0⊗1T_0\otimes1T0​⊗1. Commutation with RΓ⊗1R_\Gamma\otimes1RΓ​⊗1 makes T0∈LΓT_0\in\mathcal L_\GammaT0​∈LΓ​. This gives AAA, with the reverse inclusion immediate. □\square□

Exercise 6.12. Level 3. Derive both ambient commutants in (5B.4) and prove that no unitary on V\mathcal VV exchanges A,CA,CA,C. Which part of that proof must not be silently transferred to the stabilized copies?

Solution. Commutation with AAA puts each second-coordinate matrix coefficient in RΓR_\GammaRΓ​. Finite compressions in the unrestricted second matrix factor give A′=RΓ⊗‾B(ℓ2(Δ))A'=R_\Gamma\overline\otimes B(\ell^2(\Delta))A′=RΓ​⊗​B(ℓ2(Δ)). For C′C'C′, use the right regular product-group generators and Lemma 5A.1 to obtain LΓ⊗‾LΔ\mathcal L_\Gamma\overline\otimes\mathcal L_\DeltaLΓ​⊗​LΔ​. The first commutant contains a nonunitary isometry 1⊗s01\otimes s_01⊗s0​ obtained by bijecting the Δ\DeltaΔ-basis with a proper infinite subset. The second has the faithful tracial state at δ(e,e)\delta_{(e,e)}δ(e,e)​, obtained by inversion from the finite product-group right algebra. Any isometry vvv in it has τ0(1−vv∗)=0\tau_0(1-vv^*)=0τ0​(1−vv∗)=0, hence is unitary. A spatial conjugacy of A,CA,CA,C would conjugate their commutants and carry the nonunitary isometry to the finite one, which is impossible. This distinguishes their actual representations before stabilization. Additional infinite matrix coordinates change those ambient commutants; the calculation does not establish an obstruction for every new stabilized representation or every possible source pair. □\square□

Exercise 6.13. Level 3. Compute JZJJZJJZJ and the two compositions on δa2⊗δe\delta_{a_2}\otimes\delta_eδa2​​⊗δe​. Prove all three assertions about intersection, generation and failure of commutation for both C,DC,DC,D and C^,D^\widehat C,\widehat DC,D. State the exact source conclusion.

Solution. The first JJJ gives (x−1,qπ(x)−1)(x^{-1},q\pi(x)^{-1})(x−1,qπ(x)−1); ZZZ appends b0−1b_0^{-1}b0−1​ on the right, and the final JJJ restores xxx and appends π(x)\pi(x)π(x). Thus Y=JZJY=JZJY=JZJ has (5B.6). For x=a2,q=ex=a_2,q=ex=a2​,q=e, use π(a2)=b1\pi(a_2)=b_1π(a2​)=b1​. The outputs of ZYZYZY and YZYZYZ are the two reduced words in (5B.7), starting with b1−1b_1^{-1}b1−1​ and b0−1b_0^{-1}b0−1​ respectively. They are distinct orthogonal basis vectors, so their difference has norm 2\sqrt22​. Since Z∈C,Y∈DZ\in C,Y\in DZ∈C,Y∈D, these algebras do not commute. Their intersection commutes with A∨B=EA\vee B=EA∨B=E and lies in EEE, so is scalar. Their join contains BBB and AAA, so is EEE.

For the stabilized copies, the full matrix commutant calculation gives (5B.9). The original internal symmetry swaps them. Their join contains P,QP,QP,Q, hence is M~\widetilde MM; their intersection is its centre and is scalar. Tensoring Z,YZ,YZ,Y with the two identity operators retains the same orthogonal-vector commutator and its lower bound 2\sqrt22​. Simultaneous closure therefore preserves the flip and generation but fails the source's commutation requirement. This rules out those repair operations for the displayed pair, including its transported whole-factor realization. It does not refute Connes's existential claim for all possible pairs. □\square□

Exercise 6.14. Level 3. In Lemma 5C.3, prove the product trace without assuming a product state in advance. Explain where joint generation is used to place a hypothetical compressed flip inside the spatial tensor product.

Solution. For b≥0b\ge0b≥0 in BBB, commutation makes ab≥0ab\ge0ab≥0 when a≥0a\ge0a≥0, so fb(a)=t(ab)f_b(a)=t(ab)fb​(a)=t(ab) is positive and normal. Since AAA is a factor, trace uniqueness gives fb=t(b)tAf_b=t(b)t_Afb​=t(b)tA​, with the scalar determined at 111. Linear decomposition into positive elements extends this to every bbb.

For algebraic sums, applying this identity to ai∗ajbi∗bja_i^*a_jb_i^*b_jai∗​aj​bi∗​bj​ proves that multiplication preserves the product L2L^2L2-inner product. Its range contains all products, and Kaplansky density makes their span dense in L2(A∨B,t)L^2(A\vee B,t)L2(A∨B,t). The resulting unitary intertwines the left regular representations, giving the normal spatial isomorphism onto the join. In Theorem 5C.4, joint generation supplies rMr=(rPr)∨(rQr)rMr=(rPr)\vee(rQr)rMr=(rPr)∨(rQr), via (5C.13). It therefore puts rSrrSrrSr, already an element of rMrrMrrMr, inside this spatial product. Exercise 6.15. Level 2. Prove (5C.7)–(5C.8) and explain why the same no-flip conclusion does not apply to N=Mk(C)N=M_k(\mathbb C)N=Mk​(C), k≥1k\ge1k≥1. Give its flip unitary explicitly.

Solution. Expanding A∗TnAA^*T_nAA∗Tn​A and taking the product trace gives exactly the sum in (5C.7). The orthonormal powers vnv^nvn make each first coefficient tend to zero by Bessel's inequality; Cauchy–Schwarz bounds each second coefficient by ∥bi∥2∥bj∥2\|b_i\|_2\|b_j\|_2∥bi​∥2​∥bj​∥2​. There are finitely many terms. Subtract the two inner products in (5C.8) as ⟨ζ−A,Tnζ⟩+⟨A,Tn(ζ−A)⟩\langle\zeta-A,T_n\zeta\rangle+\langle A,T_n(\zeta-A)\rangle⟨ζ−A,Tn​ζ⟩+⟨A,Tn​(ζ−A)⟩; unitarity of TnT_nTn​ and Cauchy–Schwarz give the stated bound. Density extends the limit to every vector, contradicting any nonzero fixed vector.

For matrices, Fk=∑i,j=1keij⊗eji,Fk(ξi⊗ξj)=ξj⊗ξi. F_k=\sum_{i,j=1}^k e_{ij}\otimes e_{ji}, \qquad F_k(\xi_i\otimes\xi_j)=\xi_j\otimes\xi_i. Fk​=i,j=1∑k​eij​⊗eji​,Fk​(ξi​⊗ξj​)=ξj​⊗ξi​. Thus Fk=Fk∗F_k=F_k^*Fk​=Fk∗​, Fk2=1F_k^2=1Fk2​=1, and Fk(a⊗1)Fk=1⊗aF_k(a\otimes1)F_k=1\otimes aFk​(a⊗1)Fk​=1⊗a. A finite-dimensional L2L^2L2-space cannot contain the infinite orthonormal family of powers used above. It has minimal projections, so Lemma 5C.1 does not apply. The type II\mathrm{II}II hypothesis in the finite-corner argument is essential.

Exercise 6.16. Level 3. For the pair in (5A.16), take the two projections before (5C.16). Show that each is finite in its own copy, compute the ambient trace of their product, and compare this calculation with the relative-commutant obstruction. Does Theorem 5C.4 rule out every possible source pair?

Solution. The corner of PPP cut by ppp is isomorphic to the finite factor AAA; the corner of QQQ cut by qqq is isomorphic to BBB. Thus these are finite projections in their respective copies. Their product is e⊗e⊗1Ve\otimes e\otimes1_{\mathcal V}e⊗e⊗1V​. In the decomposition E=B(ℓ2(Γ))⊗‾RΔE=B(\ell^2(\Gamma))\overline\otimes R_\DeltaE=B(ℓ2(Γ))⊗​RΔ​, its trace is Tr⁡L(e)2 Tr⁡ℓ2(Γ)(1) τΔ(1)=1⋅∞⋅1=∞. \operatorname{Tr}_L(e)^2\, \operatorname{Tr}_{\ell^2(\Gamma)}(1)\, \tau_\Delta(1)=1\cdot\infty\cdot1=\infty. TrL​(e)2Trℓ2(Γ)​(1)τΔ​(1)=1⋅∞⋅1=∞. The necessary trace condition is therefore satisfied. Proposition 5A.6 and Theorem 5A.7 still supply an extra relative-commutant unitary, so this pair fails a different source clause. Theorem 5C.4 excludes a finite ambient-trace product for any generating internally exchanged type II∞\mathrm{II}_\inftyII∞​ pair; Corollary 5C.5 excludes finite trace-scaling endomorphisms. Endomorphisms with infinite ambient trace on every nonzero image projection have not been excluded. The existential source assertion remains open.

Exercise 6.17. Level 2. Why does Theorem 5D.2 not require faithful states? For the vector state ω(x)=⟨ξ1,xξ1⟩\omega(x)=\langle\xi_1,x\xi_1\rangleω(x)=⟨ξ1​,xξ1​⟩ on M2(C)M_2(\mathbb C)M2​(C), identify its GNS space and representation, and exhibit a nonzero element with zero GNS vector.

Equation (5D.6) therefore gives a well-defined isometry on the quotient GNS spaces without requiring faithful vector functionals.

No faithfulness assumption on EPE_PEP​, ϕ\phiϕ or χ\chiχ is used.

For the diffuse finite spatial pair, the slice map id⊗τ\mathrm{id}\otimes\tauid⊗τ is a normal expectation onto PPP, and τ⊗τ\tau\otimes\tauτ⊗τ is a normal product state. The two copies commute and generate, but Lemma 5C.2 says that their flip is not implemented by a unitary inside their join. Thus the internal-symmetry hypothesis fails. For matrices the flip unitary FkF_kFk​ in Exercise 6.15 is internal and the expectation exists. The diffuse type II\mathrm{II}II hypothesis then fails. Neither example contradicts Theorem 5D.4.

Exercise 6.19. Level 3. Apply Theorem 5D.4 first to A,B⊂EA,B\subset EA,B⊂E in Section 5A and then to P,Q⊂M~P,Q\subset\widetilde MP,Q⊂M. List the source clauses these pairs satisfy and explain why the absence of normal expectations neither repairs their commutants nor refutes the existence of a different source pair.

Solution. Lemmas 5A.2–5A.3 give finite diffuse factors A,BA,BA,B, Theorem 5A.4 gives their factorial join EEE, and Lemma 5A.5 gives the internal self-adjoint involution JJJ exchanging them. They commute, so Theorem 5D.4 excludes normal expectations from EEE onto either factor and normal states factorizing across them. After stabilization, Theorem 5A.7 gives commuting type II∞\mathrm{II}_\inftyII∞​ copies of the entire factor, with the internal SSS, normal endomorphism and joint generation. The same expectation and product-state exclusions apply.

The unitary ZZZ, and its stabilized version, still belongs to a relative commutant outside the other copy. Hence those pairs continue to fail mutual relative-commutant equality. Sections 5C–5D provide necessary conditions for every other proposed type II∞\mathrm{II}_\inftyII∞​ source pair; they do not provide sufficiency. Connes's source assertion asks for no normal expectation, so the new exclusion leaves its unrestricted existential parent open.

Exercise 6.20. Level 2. Explain why replacing the product state in Theorem 5D.2 with an entangled normal spatial state does not avoid Theorem 5E.2. Solution. Agreement on every a⊗ba\otimes ba⊗b includes agreement on each ai∗aj⊗bi∗bja_i^*a_j\otimes b_i^*b_jai∗​aj​⊗bi∗​bj​. These are exactly the cross terms in the GNS inner product (5E.3), so the quotient isometry and its full dense range do not require a product state. Factoriality makes both normal GNS representations faithful even if the states are not faithful. Joint generation then gives the full spatial multiplication isomorphism, contradicting the finite flip obstruction in type II.

The displayed matrix vector state is normal and is not a product state: its value on e11⊗e22e_{11}\otimes e_{22}e11​⊗e22​ is zero, while its two marginal values are each 1/21/21/2, whose product is 1/41/41/4. The actual algebra may be the spatial matrix tensor product itself, with multiplication the identity on its two legs and ψ=Ω\psi=\Omegaψ=Ω. Its flip is the internal matrix flip F2F_2F2​ from Exercise 6.15. Here (5E.1) holds and the GNS conclusion is correct. The diffuse type II hypothesis of Theorem 5E.2 fails, so there is no contradiction.

Exercise 6.21. Level 3. Show that joint generation is indispensable in Theorem 5E.2 and Proposition 5E.3, even with diffuse finite copies and an internal self-adjoint flip. Use a diffuse finite factor DDD, its trace Hilbert space HD=L2(D,τ)H_D=L^2(D,\tau)HD​=L2(D,τ), H0=HD⊗HDH_0=H_D\otimes H_DH0​=HD​⊗HD​, and H=H0⊕H0\mathcal H=H_0\oplus H_0H=H0​⊕H0​.

Solution. Let λ\lambdaλ be faithful normal left multiplication on HDH_DHD​. On both summands of H\mathcal HH put P=λ(D)⊗1P=\lambda(D)\otimes1P=λ(D)⊗1 and Q=1⊗λ(D)Q=1\otimes\lambda(D)Q=1⊗λ(D), acting diagonally with the same operator in each summand. They are commuting normal diffuse finite factors. Take the ambient factor M=B(H)M=B(\mathcal H)M=B(H). If F(η⊗ζ)=ζ⊗ηF(\eta\otimes\zeta)=\zeta\otimes\etaF(η⊗ζ)=ζ⊗η, then S=F⊕FS=F\oplus FS=F⊕F belongs to MMM, is self-adjoint, has square one and exchanges P,QP,QP,Q.

Their join is the diagonal normal spatial representation of D⊗‾DD\overline\otimes DD⊗​D. It is proper in MMM: every operator in the join commutes with the projection onto the first summand, while the nonzero off-diagonal identity between the two copies of H0H_0H0​ does not. If ξτ=[1]∈HD\xi_\tau=[1]\in H_Dξτ​=[1]∈HD​, the unit vector (ξτ⊗ξτ)⊕0(\xi_\tau\otimes\xi_\tau)\oplus0(ξτ​⊗ξτ​)⊕0 defines a normal state ψ\psiψ on MMM agreeing with the normal spatial state Ω=τ⊗τ\Omega=\tau\otimes\tauΩ=τ⊗τ on every a⊗ba\otimes ba⊗b. The inclusion T:H0→HT:H_0\to\mathcal HT:H0​→H, Tη=η⊕0T\eta=\eta\oplus0Tη=η⊕0, is a nonzero bounded intertwiner for the two legs. The first-summand projection reduces the pair but does not commute with all of MMM. Thus the step from generator commutation to the full ambient commutant in (5E.6) would be false without joint generation. The finite spatial flip remains outer in the pair's join; the displayed SSS lives in the larger ambient factor. This example leaves every hypothesis and limitation of the two propositions consistent.

Exercise 6.22. Level 2. (4 points: the finite-group boundary.) For a finite group GGG of order mmm, construct a normal conditional expectation B(ℓ2G)→LGB(\ell^2G)\to\mathcal L_GB(ℓ2G)→LG​. Thus (τG∘EG)(pg)=1/m(\tau_G\circ E_G)(p_g)=1/m(τG​∘EG​)(pg​)=1/m, and the sum of all mmm masses is one. The inequality ∣F∣t≤1|F|t\le1∣F∣t≤1 does not force t=0t=0t=0 when ∣F∣≤m|F|\le m∣F∣≤m. That is exactly where the infinite-group argument ceases to apply. Award 2 points for the expectation and its range/bimodularity, 1 for the mass computation, and 1 for the failed inference.

At every finite matrix level the averages preserve positive matrices and the positive cone is ultraweakly closed, so EEE is completely positive. Also E(1)=1E(1)=1E(1)=1.

For fixed k∈Gk\in Gk∈G, eventually k∈Gnk\in G_nk∈Gn​, and then ρkEn(x)ρk∗=En(x)\rho_kE_n(x)\rho_k^*=E_n(x)ρk​En​(x)ρk∗​=En​(x). Taking the ultraweak limit gives the same equality for E(x)E(x)E(x). Lemma 5A.1 therefore puts its range in LG\mathcal L_GLG​. Every EnE_nEn​ fixes LG\mathcal L_GLG​, so EEE fixes it too. Multiplication by a fixed bounded operator is ultraweakly continuous, and all ρh\rho_hρh​ commute with LG\mathcal L_GLG​. The bimodularity of every EnE_nEn​ consequently passes to EEE. Thus EEE is a conditional expectation.

For the rank-one projection pgp_gpg​, the projections ρhpgρh∗=pgh−1\rho_hp_g\rho_h^*=p_{gh^{-1}}ρh​pg​ρh∗​=pgh−1​, h∈Gnh\in G_nh∈Gn​, are mutually orthogonal. Hence ∥En(pg)∥=∣Gn∣−1⟶0,E(pg)=0. \|E_n(p_g)\|=|G_n|^{-1}\longrightarrow0, \qquad E(p_g)=0. ∥En​(pg​)∥=∣Gn​∣−1⟶0,E(pg​)=0. Finite sums of the pgp_gpg​'s have image zero. Increasing such sums through an enumeration of GGG gives the identity strongly, whereas E(1)=1E(1)=1E(1)=1. Therefore EEE is not normal. Exercise 6.24. Level 2. (6 points: the finite-matrix boundary.) For scalars caic_{ai}cai​, positivity gives the positive operator ∑a,b=1r∑i,j=1mcai‾ Xijab cbj ≥0on K. \sum_{a,b=1}^r\sum_{i,j=1}^m \overline{c_{ai}}\,X^{ab}_{ij}\,c_{bj}\ \ge0 \quad\hbox{on }K. a,b=1∑r​i,j=1∑m​cai​​Xijab​cbj​ ≥0on K. The range lies in NNN, and Fϕ(a⊗1K)=a⊗1KF_\phi(a\otimes1_K)=a\otimes1_KFϕ​(a⊗1K​)=a⊗1K​ for every a∈Mm(C)a\in M_m(\mathbb C)a∈Mm​(C). Hence FϕF_\phiFϕ​ is idempotent onto NNN. For the normalized trace τN(a⊗1K)=m−1Tr⁡m(a)\tau_N(a\otimes1_K)=m^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}_m(a)τN​(a⊗1K​)=m−1Trm​(a), (τN∘Fϕ)(X)=1m∑i=1mTr⁡K(dϕXii)=Tr⁡Cm⊗K(dX),d=m−11m⊗dϕ. \begin{aligned} (\tau_N\circ F_\phi)(X) &=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{Tr}_K(d_\phi X_{ii})\\ &=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb C^m\otimes K}(dX),\\ d&=m^{-1}1_m\otimes d_\phi. \end{aligned} (τN​∘Fϕ​)(X)d​=m1​i=1∑m​TrK​(dϕ​Xii​)=TrCm⊗K​(dX),=m−11m​⊗dϕ​.​ Thus d=m−11m⊗dϕd=m^{-1}1_m\otimes d_\phid=m−11m​⊗dϕ​ is a nonzero positive trace-class operator of trace one commuting with NNN. The algebra NNN has vector-space dimension m2m^2m2, irrespective of the dimension of KKK; it fails the infinite-dimensional-factor hypothesis of Lemma 5G.1. Exercise 6.25. Level 2. (6 points: every commuting positive trace-class operator vanishes.) Let N0⊂B(K)N_0\subset B(K)N0​⊂B(K) be a normally and unitally represented infinite-dimensional finite factor, with no separability assumption on KKK. Prove that a positive trace-class operator T∈N0′T\in N_0'T∈N0′​ must be zero. Treat every positive eigenvalue and explain why the compact spectral theorem finishes the argument without assuming Tr⁡K(T)=1\operatorname{Tr}_K(T)=1TrK​(T)=1.

Solution. For each positive eigenvalue μ>0\mu>0μ>0 of TTT, compactness makes Kμ=ker⁡(T−μ1)K_\mu=\ker(T-\mu1)Kμ​=ker(T−μ1) finite-dimensional. Its spectral projection eμ=1{μ}(T)e_\mu=1_{\{\mu\}}(T)eμ​=1{μ}​(T) commutes with N0N_0N0​, because TTT does. If Kμ≠{0}K_\mu\ne\{0\}Kμ​={0}, restriction is a nonzero normal unital representation πμ:N0⟶B(Kμ). \pi_\mu:N_0\longrightarrow B(K_\mu). πμ​:N0​⟶B(Kμ​). The kernel is an ultraweakly closed two-sided ideal N0zμN_0z_\muN0​zμ​ for a central projection zμz_\muzμ​. Factoriality makes zμz_\muzμ​ zero or one, and unitality on the nonzero space rules out one. Thus πμ\pi_\muπμ​ is injective, impossible because N0N_0N0​ is infinite-dimensional and B(Kμ)B(K_\mu)B(Kμ​) is finite-dimensional. The same argument rules out every positive eigenvalue.

A positive compact operator on any Hilbert space has only finite-multiplicity nonzero eigenvalues, with at most countably many of them, and is the norm limit of the sums ∑μμeμ\sum_\mu\mu e_\mu∑μ​μeμ​ over its nonzero eigenvalues. It is zero on the remaining kernel. Since no positive eigenvalue is possible and a positive operator has no negative eigenvalues, these sums are all zero and T=0T=0T=0. Equivalently, a nonzero positive compact operator would have ∥T∥>0\|T\|>0∥T∥>0 as an eigenvalue, already excluded. Normalization of the trace was never used. Award 2 points for all positive spectral projections and their finite-dimensional reducing spaces, 2 for normality and the central-ideal proof of injectivity, and 2 for the compact spectral conclusion on arbitrary KKK without a trace-one assumption.

(b) For eij=Eij⊗1ke_{ij}=E_{ij}\otimes1_keij​=Eij​⊗1k​, fij=1k⊗Eijf_{ij}=1_k\otimes E_{ij}fij​=1k​⊗Eij​, p=e11p=e_{11}p=e11​, q=f11q=f_{11}q=f11​, compute r=pqr=pqr=pq, the corner Rk=rMkrR_k=r\mathcal M_k rRk​=rMk​r, the two coefficient copies from (5H.5), and s=rFkrs=rF_k rs=rFk​r. Compute the exact positive defect for x=1k⊗E21x=1_k\otimes E_{21}x=1k​⊗E21​, and state why these finite-trace calculations do not contradict Proposition 5H.2.

Solution. (a) Set Fk=∑i,j=1kEij⊗Eji. F_k=\sum_{i,j=1}^k E_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}. Fk​=i,j=1∑k​Eij​⊗Eji​. On a basis vector δa⊗δb\delta_a\otimes\delta_bδa​⊗δb​, only the summand (i,j)=(b,a)(i,j)=(b,a)(i,j)=(b,a) is nonzero, and its image is δb⊗δa\delta_b\otimes\delta_aδb​⊗δa​. Thus FkF_kFk​ exchanges the tensor coordinates, is unitary, has square one, and is self-adjoint. Directly on the same basis, Fk(a⊗1k)Fk=1k⊗a(a∈Mk(C)), F_k(a\otimes1_k)F_k=1_k\otimes a\qquad(a\in M_k(\mathbb C)), Fk​(a⊗1k​)Fk​=1k​⊗a(a∈Mk​(C)), so it exchanges the two copies. Every X∈MkX\in\mathcal M_kX∈Mk​ has a first-coordinate block matrix. Commutation with the diagonal Eii⊗1kE_{ii}\otimes1_kEii​⊗1k​ kills its off-diagonal blocks; commutation with all Eij⊗1kE_{ij}\otimes1_kEij​⊗1k​ then makes its diagonal blocks equal. Grading: 2 points for the general compression formula and both full ranges; 2 points for the exact commutator and its norm; 2 points for both positive defects and the precise closure and scope comparison.

7. Source comparison and remaining scope

Connes's author-hosted Corollary 11, PDF 44–45, assumes a properly infinite random-operator factor on a principal measurable groupoid and asks for two mutually commuting copies, each the relative commutant of the other, generating the factor and exchanged by a symmetry of square one. The source leaves the proof as an exercise and mentions the equivalence of the field with its tensor square.

The full current Claude-SQ Proposition 8.5 constructs the tensor pair and proves relative-commutant equality under the actual standing standard Borel hypothesis of Section 8. Its Remark 8.6 explicitly does not prove generation. Commuting copies in principal groupoid factors, Sections 1–4, supplies the standard Borel generation proof and semifinite factor-support reduction. Neither proof is contradicted by the present construction.

The present full calculation supplies a properly infinite factor at the weaker countably generated, point-separated, faithful proper, sigma-finite scope. It demonstrates that the factor premise does not restore the missing fibre-density step, and exhibits the precise extra relative-commutant operator for the canonical tensor construction. An existential counterexample or a different full construction would still be needed to settle Connes's broader Corollary 11. Its source parent remains open; the other recorded source obligations and final prerequisite/source validation remain.
